chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from al-Hasan ibn Ali from Ahmad ibn A'idh from Abu Khadijah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding two enslaved men who have been granted autonomy (mukatab) and are permitted to buy and sell with their own wealth, and there was a dispute between them, so this one ran to the master of that one, and that one ran to the master of this one, and they were equal in strength.

So this one bought the slave from the master of that one, and that one went and bought the other slave from the master of this one, so they returned to their place, and each one clung to his companion and said to him, 'You are my slave, I have bought you from your master.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'A judgment is made between them from where they separated; the path is measured. Whichever one was closer, he is the one who preceded the one who was farther. And if they were equal, they return to their masters, because they arrived equally and separated equally. Unless one of them preceded his companion, then the predecessor is entitled to him; if he wishes, he sells him, and if he wishes, he keeps him, and he is not allowed to harm him.'
ai.seo_question: How is ownership determined when two enslaved men buy each other's freedom simultaneously?
ai.summary: This ruling from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the specific case of two enslaved men who purchase each other's freedom, establishing that ownership is determined by physical proximity at the point of separation rather than mere intent. The principle of 'measuring the path' ensures legal clarity in disputes, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on tangible evidence in manumission transactions. It highlights the balance between the slaves' agency in buying freedom and the masters' rights, ensuring no party is unjustly deprived.
